items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 13.6 Why sometimes sounds travelling across water are louder than we expect

items.label: list_item
items.text: Most of the sound we hear travels to us in a straight line(Path B).

items.label: list_item
items.text: But some sound travels upwards(Path A).

items.label: list_item
items.text: If the temperature conditionsareright,then as the sound waves travel through theair they arerefracted and followa curvedpath downwards(Path C).

items.label: list_item
items.text: So the sound wehearseems louder and clearer.

items.label: text
items.text: Small objects,such as the strings of the violin in Figure 13.7,vibrate quickly and produce sound waveswith a high frequency.These sounds areheard as noteswith a high pitch.

items.label: text
items.text: Larger objects,such as the strings of the cello,vibratemore slowly and producewaveswitha lower frequency.Thesesoundshave alowerpitch.

items.label: text
items.text: The frequencyofa source is thenumberof completevibrationsit makes each second.We measure frequency in hertz(Hz).If a source hasa frequency of 50Hzthismeans thatitvibrates50 timeseachsecond and thereforeproduces 50waveseachsecond.

items.label: text
items.text: Although we cannot see an actual sound wave,we can see an image or representation ofitbyconnectingamicrophone toapieceofapparatus calledanoscilloscope.When the sound wave froma source suchas a tuning fork orvibrating string enters the microphone,the oscilloscope 'draws'the longitudinal soundwave asa transversewavewhichallowsus tosee featuressuchas the wave's amplitude and frequency moreeasily.
